# Book I, Proposition 24

*The wider angle has the longer base*

> If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the base greater than the base.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/24-idea.svg" alt="Two triangles with the same two sides (blue and red): open the angle between them wider (yellow), and the base (black) comes out longer." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Two triangles with the same two sides (blue and red): open the angle between them wider (yellow), and the base (black) comes out longer.</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/24.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.24, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF, and let the angle at A be greater than the angle at D;

I say that the base BC is also greater than the base EF.

For, since the angle BAC is greater than the angle EDF, let there be constructed, on the straight line DE, and at the point D on it, the angle EDG equal to the angle BAC; [I. 23]

let DG be made equal to either of the two straight lines AC, DF, and let EG, FG be joined.

Then, since AB is equal to DE, and AC to DG,

the two sides BA, AC are equal to the two sides ED, DG, respectively;

and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDG;

therefore the base BC is equal to the base EG. [I. 4]

Again, since DF is equal to DG,

the angle DGF is also equal to the angle DFG; [I. 5]

therefore the angle DFG is greater than the angle EGF.

Therefore the angle EFG is much greater than the angle EGF.

And, since EFG is a triangle having the angle EFG greater than the angle EGF,

and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]

the side EG is also greater than EF.

But EG is equal to BC.

Therefore BC is also greater than EF.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- "Let DG be made equal to DF." Euclid cites nothing here. On the ray from `D`
through any point `P` there is a point `G` with `DG` equal to `DF`: describe the circle
with centre `D` and distance `DF` (Post. 3); the straight line `DP`, which passes
through its centre, cuts it on `P`'s side of `D` (System E, Intersections 5, with a
point `Q` set out on the other side); and `DG` is a radius [Def. 15]. -/
theorem Prop24.made_equal {D F P : Point} (hDF : D ≠ F) (hDP : D ≠ P) :
    ∃ G : Point, OnRay G D P ∧ ‖D G‖ = ‖D F‖ := by
  obtain ⟨α, hD_α, hF_α⟩ := Postulate3 D F hDF
  obtain ⟨L, hD_L, hP_L⟩ := Postulate1 D P hDP
  /- A point `Q` behind `D`, so that the circle is cut on `P`'s side. -/
  obtain ⟨Q, hPDQ⟩ := produce hDP.symm
  have hQ_L : OnLine Q L := on_line_of_between hPDQ hP_L hD_L
  obtain ⟨G, hG_α, hG_L, hGDQ⟩ :=
    line_circle_beyond (centre_inside hD_α) hD_L hQ_L (ne_of_between (between_symm hPDQ))
  refine ⟨G, ⟨hDP, ne_of_between hGDQ, ⟨L, hD_L, hP_L, hG_L⟩, fun hGDP => ?_⟩,
    Definition15 hD_α hG_α hF_α⟩
  /- `G` and `P` are both on the far side of `D` from `Q`, so `D` is not between them. -/
  exact not_between_of_between_between hGDQ hGDP (between_symm hPDQ)

/-- A point `G` on the ray from `D` through `P` is on the same side of `DE` as `P`:
the ray leaves `DE` at `D` and never crosses it again (System E, Pasch 4). -/
theorem Prop24.side {D E F G P : Point} (hG : OnRay G D P) (hP : SameSideOf P F D E) :
    SameSideOf G F D E := by
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hP.1
  obtain ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hPF : SameSide P F L := hP.sameSide hD_L hE_L
  have hP_L : ¬ OnLine P L := not_on_line_of_same_side hPF
  obtain ⟨-, hGD, ⟨M, hD_M, hP_M, hG_M⟩, hGDP⟩ := hG
  have hLM : L ≠ M := fun e => hP_L (e ▸ hP_M)
  have hGP : SameSide G P L := by
    by_cases hGP : G = P
    · subst hGP
      exact same_side_refl hP_L
    · /- Were `G` and `P` on opposite sides of `DE`, `D` would lie between them. -/
      refine Classical.byContradiction fun hs => hGDP ?_
      exact pasch4 hLM hD_L hD_M hG_M hP_M hGP hGD (fun e => hP_L (e ▸ hD_L)) hs
  exact SameSideOf.of_line hDE hD_L hE_L (same_side_trans (same_side_symm hGP) hPF)

/-- `F` lies within the angle `EDG`. Both are on one side of `DE`, and the angle `EDF`
is the less. If `F` were on `DG`, the angle `EDF` would be the angle `EDG`
(`angle_onRay_right`); if it were beyond `DG`, then `G` would lie within the angle
`EDF` (System E, Triple incidence 2), and the angle `EDG` would be a part of it
(`Prop16.part`), so the greater would be less than the less. -/
theorem Prop24.within {D E F G : Point} (hGF : SameSideOf G F D E) (h : ∠ E D F < ∠ E D G) :
    SameSideOf F E D G := by
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hGF.1
  obtain ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hGF_L : SameSide G F L := hGF.sameSide hD_L hE_L
  have hG_L : ¬ OnLine G L := not_on_line_of_same_side hGF_L
  have hF_L : ¬ OnLine F L := not_on_line_of_same_side (same_side_symm hGF_L)
  have hDG : D ≠ G := fun e => hG_L (e ▸ hD_L)
  have hDF : D ≠ F := fun e => hF_L (e ▸ hD_L)
  obtain ⟨M, hD_M, hG_M⟩ := Postulate1 D G hDG
  refine SameSideOf.of_line hDG hD_M hG_M (Classical.byContradiction fun hs => ?_)
  by_cases hF_M : OnLine F M
  · /- `F` on `DG`, and on `G`'s side of `D`, since both are on one side of `DE`. -/
    have hF_ray : OnRay F D G :=
      ⟨hDG, hDF.symm, ⟨M, hD_M, hG_M, hF_M⟩, fun hb => pasch3 hb hD_L (same_side_symm hGF_L)⟩
    rw [angle_onRay_right hF_ray hDE.symm] at h
    exact lt_irrefl _ h
  · obtain ⟨N, hD_N, hF_N⟩ := Postulate1 D F hDF
    have hEG_N : SameSide E G N :=
      triple_incidence2 hD_L hD_M hD_N hE_L hG_M hF_N hGF_L
        (fun h' => hs (same_side_symm h')) hF_M hDE.symm
    obtain ⟨hadd, hpos⟩ :=
      Prop16.part hGF (SameSideOf.of_line hDF hD_N hF_N (same_side_symm hEG_N))
    have hlt := CommonNotion5 (a := ∠ E D G) hpos
    rw [← hadd] at hlt
    exact lt_irrefl _ (lt_trans hlt h)

/-- Where `F` falls. Since `F` lies within the angle `EDG`, the straight line `DF`,
drawn on, crosses `EG` at some point `X` (`crossbar`). Then either `F` is `X`, and lies
on `EG`; or `F` is short of `X`, within the triangle `DEG`; or `F` is beyond `X`, on
the far side of `EG` from `D`, and `EFG` is a triangle. The last is Euclid's figure. -/
theorem Prop24.cases {D E F G : Point} (hGF : SameSideOf G F D E) (hFE : SameSideOf F E D G) :
    Between E F G ∨ InsideTriangle F G D E ∨
      ∃ X : Point, Between E X G ∧ Between D X F ∧ Triangle E G F := by
  obtain ⟨X, hEXG, hX⟩ := crossbar hGF.symm hFE
  have hDEG : Triangle D E G := hGF.triangle
  obtain ⟨N, hE_N, hG_N⟩ := Postulate1 E G hDEG.ne₂₃
  have hX_N : OnLine X N := on_line_of_between_ends hEXG hE_N hG_N
  have hD_N : ¬ OnLine D N := hDEG.bca.off_line hE_N hG_N
  by_cases hXF : X = F
  · subst hXF
    exact Or.inl hEXG
  obtain ⟨hDF, hXD, ⟨L, hD_L, hF_L, hX_L⟩, hXDF⟩ := hX
  /- `F` is off `EG`: otherwise `DF` and `EG` would be one straight line, through `D`. -/
  have hF_N : ¬ OnLine F N := fun hF_N => hD_N (line_unique hXF hX_L hF_L hX_N hF_N ▸ hD_L)
  rcases between_cases hXD.symm hXF hDF hD_L hX_L hF_L with hDXF | hb | hDFX
  · exact Or.inr (Or.inr ⟨X, hEXG, hDXF, Triangle.of_line hE_N hG_N hDEG.ne₂₃ hF_N⟩)
  · exact absurd hb hXDF
  · /- `F` is on `D`'s side of `EG` (Pasch 2), and within the angle `EDG`. -/
    exact Or.inr (Or.inl ⟨hGF.symm,
      SameSideOf.of_line hDEG.ne₂₃ hE_N hG_N (pasch2 (between_symm hDFX) hX_N hF_N), hFE.swap⟩)

/-- The part is less than the whole, for angles: if `R` lies between `P` and `Q`, and
`V` is off `PQ`, the angle `RVQ` is less than the angle `PVQ`, for `PVQ` is made up of
`PVR` and `RVQ` (`angle_add_of_between`), and `PVR` is something, since `R` is off
`VP` (System E, Diagram-angle 1). [C.N. 5] -/
theorem Prop24.part {V P Q R : Point} (hPQV : Triangle P Q V) (h : Between P R Q) :
    ∠ R V Q < ∠ P V Q := by
  rw [angle_add_of_between hPQV h, add_comm]
  apply CommonNotion5
  obtain ⟨N, hP_N, hQ_N⟩ := Postulate1 P Q (ne_of_between_ends h)
  have hV_N : ¬ OnLine V N := hPQV.off_line hP_N hQ_N
  have hR_N : OnLine R N := on_line_of_between_ends h hP_N hQ_N
  have hVP : V ≠ P := fun e => hV_N (e ▸ hP_N)
  have hVR : V ≠ R := fun e => hV_N (e ▸ hR_N)
  obtain ⟨L, hV_L, hP_L⟩ := Postulate1 V P hVP
  refine Magnitude.pos_of_ne_zero fun h0 => ?_
  have hR_L : OnLine R L := (same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero hVP hVR hV_L hP_L h0).1
  exact hV_N (line_unique (ne_of_between h) hP_L hR_L hP_N hR_N ▸ hV_L)

/-- If `a` and `b` together are less than `a` and `c` together, then `b` is less than
`c`: take the common `a` away. Otherwise `c` would be equal to `b` or less, and adding
`a` to each would keep it so (System E §3.5, the laws of magnitudes). -/
theorem Prop24.less {k : Kind} {a b c : Magnitude k} (h : a + b < a + c) : b < c := by
  rcases lt_trichotomy b c with h' | h' | h'
  · exact h'
  · subst h'
    exact absurd h (lt_irrefl _)
  · have h'' := add_lt_add_right a h'
    rw [add_comm c a, add_comm b a] at h''
    exact absurd (lt_trans h h'') (lt_irrefl _)

/-- If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the
angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the
base greater than the base. -/
theorem Prop24 {A B C D E F : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hDEF : Triangle D E F)
    (hAB : ‖A B‖ = ‖D E‖) (hAC : ‖A C‖ = ‖D F‖) (h : ∠ E D F < ∠ B A C) :
    ‖E F‖ < ‖B C‖ := by
  -- Let ABC, DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF
  -- respectively, namely AB to DE, and AC to DF, and let the angle at A be greater than the
  -- angle at D;
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hDEF.ne₁₂
  have hDF : D ≠ F := hDEF.ne₁₃
  -- I say that the base BC is also greater than the base EF.
  -- For, since the angle BAC is greater than the angle EDF, let there be constructed, on the
  -- straight line DE, and at the point D on it, the angle EDG equal to the angle BAC; [I. 23]
  /- I.23 builds the angle at `D` with one arm along the ray from `D` through `E` (it
     passes through a point `E₁` of that ray) and the other through a point `G₁` on
     whichever side of `DE` we ask for. We ask for `F`'s side, as in Euclid's figure. -/
  obtain ⟨E₁, G₁, hE₁, hG₁F, hE₁DG₁⟩ := Prop23 hDE hABC.bac hDEF
  -- let DG be made equal to either of the two straight lines AC, DF, and let EG, FG be joined.
  /- `G` is laid along the arm `DG₁` with a circle about `D` (`Prop24.made_equal`). It is
     on `F`'s side of `DE`, as `G₁` is (`Prop24.side`), and the angle `EDG` is the angle
     `E₁DG₁`, its arms being the same rays (`angle_eq_of_onRay`). -/
  obtain ⟨G, hG, hDG_DF⟩ := Prop24.made_equal hDF hG₁F.triangle.ne₁₃
  have hGF : SameSideOf G F D E := Prop24.side hG hG₁F
  have hEDG : ∠ E D G = ∠ B A C := (angle_eq_of_onRay hE₁.symm hG).trans hE₁DG₁
  /- Joining needs different points. `G` is off `DE`; and `F`, the angle `EDF` being the
     less, lies within the angle `EDG` (`Prop24.within`), so it is off `DG`. -/
  have hFE : SameSideOf F E D G := Prop24.within hGF (by rw [hEDG]; exact h)
  have hDEG : Triangle D E G := hGF.triangle
  have hDFG : Triangle D F G := hFE.triangle.acb
  -- Then, since AB is equal to DE, and AC to DG,
  have hAC_DG : ‖A C‖ = ‖D G‖ := hAC.trans hDG_DF.symm
  -- the two sides BA, AC are equal to the two sides ED, DG, respectively;
  -- and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDG;
  have hBAC : ∠ B A C = ∠ E D G := hEDG.symm
  -- therefore the base BC is equal to the base EG. [I. 4]
  have hBC_EG : ‖B C‖ = ‖E G‖ := (Prop4 hABC hDEG hAB hAC_DG hBAC).1
  -- Again, since DF is equal to DG,
  have hDF_DG : ‖D F‖ = ‖D G‖ := hDG_DF.symm
  -- the angle DGF is also equal to the angle DFG; [I. 5]
  /- Our I.5 is stated as Euclid states it, with the equal sides produced, so `DF` and
     `DG` are produced to `K` and `H` in order to cite it. Only the angles at the base
     are used. -/
  obtain ⟨K, hDFK⟩ := produce hDF
  obtain ⟨H, hDGH⟩ := produce hDEG.ne₁₃
  have hDGF : ∠ D G F = ∠ D F G := (Prop5 hDFG hDF_DG hDFK hDGH).1.symm
  /- Euclid's figure has `F` beyond `EG`. Lean must also take the two cases he leaves to
     the reader (`Prop24.cases`), and it takes them as Proclus does. -/
  have hEF_EG : ‖E F‖ < ‖E G‖ := by
    rcases Prop24.cases hGF hFE with hEFG | hF | ⟨X, hEXG, hDXF, hEGF⟩
    · /- `F` falls on `EG`: "it is then obvious that EG is greater than EF", the whole
         than the part. -/
      exact len_lt_of_between hEFG
    · /- `F` falls within the triangle `DEG`: "by I. 21, DF, FE are together less than
         DG, GE. But DF is equal to DG; therefore EF is less than EG." -/
      have hI21 : ‖D F‖ + ‖F E‖ < ‖D G‖ + ‖G E‖ := (Prop21 hDEG.cab hF).1
      rw [hDF_DG] at hI21
      rw [len_symm E F, len_symm E G]
      exact Prop24.less hI21
    · /- Euclid's figure: `F` beyond `EG`, which `DF` crosses at `X`. -/
      have hFG : F ≠ G := hDFG.ne₂₃
      have hEG : E ≠ G := hDEG.ne₂₃
      -- therefore the angle DFG is greater than the angle EGF.
      /- The angle `EGF` is the angle `XGF`, a part of the angle `DGF`, since `X` lies
         between `D` and `F` (`Prop24.part`). -/
      have hEGF_DGF : ∠ E G F < ∠ D G F := by
        rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hEXG)) hFG]
        exact Prop24.part hDFG hDXF
      have hEGF_DFG : ∠ E G F < ∠ D F G := by
        rw [← hDGF]
        exact hEGF_DGF
      -- Therefore the angle EFG is much greater than the angle EGF.
      /- The angle `DFG` is the angle `XFG`, a part of the angle `EFG`, since `X` lies
         between `E` and `G`. -/
      have hDFG_EFG : ∠ D F G < ∠ E F G := by
        rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between (between_symm hDXF)) hFG.symm]
        exact Prop24.part hEGF hEXG
      have hmuch : ∠ E G F < ∠ E F G := lt_trans hEGF_DFG hDFG_EFG
      -- And, since EFG is a triangle having the angle EFG greater than the angle EGF,
      have hEFG : Triangle E F G := hEGF.acb
      -- and the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, [I. 19]
      -- the side EG is also greater than EF.
      exact Prop19 hEFG (by rw [angle_symm hFG hEG]; exact hmuch)
  -- But EG is equal to BC.
  rw [hBC_EG]
  -- Therefore BC is also greater than EF.
  exact hEF_EG
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26): The angle `ABC` is the angle `CBA`. (Metric 4)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35): The triangle `ABC` is the triangle `CAB`. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38): The triangle `ABC` is the triangle `ACB`. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, then `AB` and `BC` together make up `AC`. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The line `AB` is the line `BA`. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle `BAC` is nothing, `C` lies on the ray from `A` through `B`. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L29): **Superposition.** The triangle `ABC` can be applied to the straight line `L` with `A` on `D`, `B` on the ray from `D` through `G`, and `C` on the side of `L` where `H` is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L22): Adding is associative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L25): Adding is commutative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L44): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L28): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L31): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L34): "Less than" is transitive. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L38): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L41): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

**One case, and the hardest.** Euclid draws F below EG and argues from that figure alone. To spare the reader the other cases, Robert Simson added a sentence of his own, "Of the two sides DE, DF let DE be the side which is not greater than the other", and Heath leaves it out: "I doubt whether Euclid could have been induced to insert the words himself, even if it had been represented to him that their omission meant leaving two possible cases out of consideration. His habit and that of the great Greek geometers was, not to set out all possible cases, but to give as a rule one case, generally the most difficult, as here, and to leave the others to the reader to work out for himself. We have already seen one instance in I. 7" (vol. 1, p. 297).

**Where F falls.** Lean can't leave anything to the reader, so it has to find out where F can be. First, F lies within the angle EDG, because the angle EDF is the less: `Prop24.within`. Were F on DG, the two angles would be one angle (`angle_onRay_right`); were it beyond DG, then G would lie within the angle EDF (System E's triple incidence rule 2), and the angle EDG would be a part of it (`Prop16.part`). Then Book Zero's `crossbar` says that DF, drawn on, crosses EG at some point X. `Prop24.cases` reads off the three possibilities: F is X itself, on EG; or F falls short of X, within the triangle DEG; or F lies beyond X, below EG, which is Euclid's figure.

**Proclus' two cases.** "Proclus of course gives the other two cases which arise if we do not first provide that DE is not greater than DF. (1) In the first case G may fall on EF produced, and it is then obvious that EG is greater than EF. (2) In the second case EG may fall below EF. If so, by I. 21, DF, FE are together less than DG, GE. But DF is equal to DG; therefore EF is less than EG, i.e. than BC." Heath adds that these "are therefore decidedly simpler than the case taken by Euclid as typical, and could well be left to the ingenuity of the learner" (vol. 1, p. 297). The Lean takes them just as Proclus does. The first is `len_lt_of_between`, the whole greater than the part. The second cites I.21, which is why I.21 is on the certificate although Euclid never mentions it. Taking the equal DF and DG away from the two sums is `Prop24.less`, one of the laws of magnitudes that System E spells out and Euclid uses without a word.

**Euclid's case: two parts and two wholes.** Euclid says "therefore the angle DFG is greater than the angle EGF", and then "much greater". Each step is the whole greater than the part, and the point X is what makes each one a part. The angle EGF is the angle XGF, since X lies on the ray from G through E (`angle_onRay_left`), and it is a part of the angle DGF because X lies between D and F. In the same way the angle DFG is the angle XFG, a part of the angle EFG because X lies between E and G. Both steps are `Prop24.part`: a straight line from a corner to a point of the opposite side cuts the angle in two (`angle_add_of_between`), and neither piece is nothing, since the point is off the arms (Diagram-angle 1). Then Common Notion 5. Only when F is below EG does X lie between D and F, and that is why the other two cases need arguments of their own.

**What else Lean made us say.** "Let DG be made equal to either of the two straight lines AC, DF" comes with no citation, and none is needed: `Prop24.made_equal` describes the circle with centre D and distance DF (Post. 3) and takes G where the arm of the new angle cuts it (System E, Intersections 5); the angle EDG is still the angle I.23 built, its arms being the same rays (`angle_eq_of_onRay`). Euclid's figure also puts G on the same side of DE as F. Our I.23 lets us ask for that side, and `Prop24.side` checks that a point laid along the new arm stays there. To cite I.5 the Lean produces DF and DG, because our I.5 is stated as Euclid states it, with the angles under the base, and so Postulate 2 is on the certificate. Every tacit rule used here is from the System E of Jeremy Avigad, Edward Dean and John Mumma, and LeanEuclid's careful Lean version of it, by Logan Murphy, Kaiyu Yang, Jialiang Sun, Zhaoyu Li, Anima Anandkumar and Xujie Si, was our guide.

**Simson's road.** Heath warns that Simson's extra sentence is not free: "If however after all we prefer to insert Simson's words and avoid the latter two cases, the proof is not complete unless we show that, with his assumption, F must, in the figure of the proposition, fall below EG" (vol. 1, pp. 297–298). Augustus De Morgan "would make the following proposition precede: Every straight line drawn from the vertex of a triangle to the base is less than the greater of the two sides, or than either if they are equal". Heath prefers "the method employed by Pfleiderer, Lardner, and Todhunter": let DF meet EG in H; the angle DHG is greater than DEG [I. 16], which is not less than DGE [I. 18]; "Hence DH is less than DG, [I. 19] and therefore DH is less than DF" (vol. 1, p. 298). So Simson's road needs I.16, I.18 and I.19, where Proclus' two cases need only I.21 and the whole greater than the part.

**Another proof.** "Lastly, the modern alternative proof is worth giving." Bisect the angle FDG by DH, meeting EG in H, and join HF. By I.4, HF is equal to HG, so EG is EH and HF together, and these are greater than EF by I.20 (vol. 1, p. 298). There are no cases at all.

**And the areas?** Why doesn't Euclid compare the areas, as he did in I.4? Proclus, Heath reports, "observes that inequality of the areas does not follow from the inequality of the angles contained by the equal sides", and that the areas "cannot be compared without the help of the theory of parallels". Proclus gives the answer all the same: if the angles at A and D are together equal to two right angles, the triangles are equal; "if greater than two right angles, that triangle which has the greater angle is less, and (3) if they are less, greater" (vol. 1, pp. 298–299). Heath traces it to Heron, through an-Nairizi, and saves it for I.38.

**The modern way.** By the law of cosines, BC² = AB² + AC² − 2 · AB · AC · cos A, and EF² is the same with cos D in place of cos A; the cosine falls as the angle grows from 0 to two right angles, so the greater angle gives the greater base. With vectors b and c along the equal sides, |b − c|² = |b|² + |c|² − 2 b·c, and only the dot product changes.
